name: Samaritan's Purse (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the US disaster work's share of programme spending (16%, Form 990 Part III 4b over the consolidated ministry expenses), the rest by Samaritan's Purse's 2025 spending abroad by region (Form 990 Schedule F: Sub-Saharan Africa 44%, the Middle East 14%, South America 11%, East Asia 9%, Central America and the Caribbean 8%, Ukraine 7%, Mexico 4%, South Asia 2%), each region split equally over its main programme countries (a judgment: no country split is published).
summary: Samaritan's Purse, an evangelical relief charity, spent $1.15 billion on its ministries in 2025 (audited accounts): $490 million on Operation Christmas Child's 10.9 million shoebox gifts to children abroad, $295 million on food, water, shelter and health care in crises abroad (Sudan, South Sudan, the DRC, Gaza, Ukraine, Myanmar, Jamaica), $185 million on US disaster relief and rebuilding, $72 million on mission hospitals and field hospitals, and $103 million on Christian education and other faith work, which the site's scale gives no value beyond its material aid. The result, about 0.05 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars: almost all of it is goods valued as consumption (about four months of food rations a person abroad, half of them outside famine settings, and the shoeboxes' contents at about a third of their US retail value), with few deaths averted; US rebuilding counts little because a few thousand dollars means little to a US household and most of its Helene money waits years to be spent. Every branch is built from spending, Samaritan's Purse's own counts and judged costs, and discounted for missing data; the biggest uncertainties are that discount, the shoeboxes' worth to the children and the cost per person of the relief.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Emergency relief and recovery abroad, 2025
rows.explainer: The line less the North American work: food, water, shelter, health care and livelihoods in Sudan, South Sudan, the DRC, Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, Ukraine, Myanmar, Jamaica and elsewhere.

rows.label: People who received clean water in 2025

source.title: Samaritan's Purse, 2025 Year-End Report

rows.explainer: Samaritan's Purse's own count, from 920 water points drilled or rehabilitated in 11 countries (same page). Its own count, not independently checked: implementation_adj.

rows.label: Cost per person given clean water
rows.explainer: No split of water spending is published. A hand-pump borehole in rural Africa costs about $8,000-20,000 and serves 250-500 people, rehabilitations a fraction of that; with hygiene training and staff, $30-150 a person. 274,530 people from 920 points is about 300 a point. Judgment $60 ($30-150), below World Vision's $150 for its broader water, sanitation and hygiene programmes.

rows.label: Cost per person reached elsewhere, relative to South Sudan
rows.explainer: South Sudan's response is food-heavy and costly (remote, air and river transport, $203 a person); Ukraine's and the Middle East's food parcels and winter kits cost about as much per person, Jamaica's and Myanmar's emergency kits less. Judgment 1 (0.6-1.5).

rows.label: People reached by water and hygiene in South Sudan, 2025

source.title: Samaritan's Purse, Form 990 for 2025 (IRS e-file object 202632459349300243; also at https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/581437002/202632459349300243/full)
source.quote: MORE THAN 60,000 PEOPLE RECEIVED HELP THROUGH OUR WATER, SANITATION, AND HYGIENE PROGRAMS

rows.explainer: Counted, and costed, in the water branch, so their cost is taken out of South Sudan's cost per person fed.

rows.label: Programme cost per person reached by relief abroad
rows.explainer: South Sudan's spending less its water work, over the people it fed, about $191, applied to the rest of the relief.

rows.label: Relief abroad other than clean water
People reached by relief abroad in 2025
rows.explainer: Spending over the cost per person; Samaritan's Purse publishes no total of people reached by its relief.

rows.label: Cost per person reached by relief abroad, including overhead
rows.explainer: Context: about four times World Vision's $30 a person for relief, because the rations here are larger (about four months of food in South Sudan).

rows.label: Death rate among the people reached during the crisis, without the response
rows.explainer: For the share of the people reached in famine-risk settings (Sudan, South Sudan, eastern DRC, Gaza): mortality surveys there commonly find crude death rates of 0.3-1 per 10,000 a day (0.011-0.037 a year); above 1 is the emergency threshold. Judgment 0.018 (0.012-0.035), as in World Vision's model of the same kind of food response.

rows.label: Death rate in the same populations before the crisis
rows.explainer: The site's crude death rates for three of the largest responses (UN World Population Prospects), so only excess deaths count.

rows.label: Share of the people reached who are in famine-risk settings
rows.explainer: Sub-Saharan Africa takes 44% of Samaritan's Purse's spending abroad (Form 990 Schedule F, $275M of $623M) and Gaza much of the Middle East's 14%; Ukraine, Lebanon and Syria, Myanmar and Jamaica are crises where few people reached are at risk of dying of hunger. Judgment 50% (30-70%); excess deaths averted among the rest are left out (unmodelled_benefits_adj).

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths the response averts among the people reached
rows.explainer: Food in a food crisis prevents some deaths from hunger and the infections it worsens, but most people reached are not at risk in the months covered. The Cochrane review of cash in disasters (Pega et al. 2015) found one drought study with far fewer child deaths, all very low certainty; long-running cash programmes cut under-five deaths by about 8% (Richterman et al. 2023). Judgment 10% (3-25%), as in World Vision's model.

rows.label: Kilograms per pound

source.title: NIST, Handbook 44 Appendix C, units of mass

rows.explainer: The exact definition of the avoirdupois pound, to put the food in kilograms.

rows.label: Food per person reached (kg)
rows.explainer: About 60 kg a person in South Sudan.

rows.label: Food in a full daily ration (kg)
rows.explainer: A WFP general ration of about 2,100 kcal is roughly 450-550 g of cereal, pulses and oil a day. Judgment 0.5 kg (0.4-0.6).

rows.label: Years of the crisis the response covers per person
rows.explainer: Full-ration days per person, about four months.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person reached (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Excess deaths over the months covered in famine-risk settings, times the share the response averts.

rows.label: Share of the deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: A stand-in: the site's WHO Global Health Estimates split of diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa (facts/death_ages.json), for excess crisis deaths, which are mostly hunger-worsened infections: 55% under five, within the 40-60% the family's guidance gives.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: From the same stand-in split.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: From the same stand-in split; the rest valued at the 50-74 band.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's one value of a death, by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Illness averted per person reached by relief, in DALYs (before adjustments)

source.title: Samaritan's Purse, Form 990 for 2025 (IRS e-file object 202632459349300243; also at https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/581437002/202632459349300243/full)
source.quote: OUR MEDICAL TEAMS PROVIDED OUTPATIENT SERVICES TO OVER 54,600 PEOPLE.

rows.explainer: 0: the relief's health care is a small part (54,600 consultations in South Sudan against 302,000 people fed) and the illness it averts is left in unmodelled_benefits_adj; the medical ministry's care has its own branch.

rows.label: Local market price of the food (US$ per kg)
rows.explainer: A judgment (no price bulletin checked), with this basis: the goods are valued at what they would cost in the local market, not at Samaritan's Purse's cost of buying, flying and trucking them in. The upper bound is the South Sudan response's all-in cost, $61.3M over about 18 million kg (ss_spend over ss_food_lbs × lb_to_kg), about $3.40 a kg, which also pays for staff, the water, health and livelihood work and the logistics of a country with few roads; a ration of mostly sorghum or maize with some pulses and oil is worth a fraction of that locally. Judgment $0.70 a kg ($0.40-1.20), about a fifth of the all-in cost.

rows.label: Food delivered per person, at local prices (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: About $41 in 2024 prices, the price year of the consumption figures; the rest of the cost per person is transport, storage, staff and the health, water and livelihood work around the food.

rows.label: Kenya: survey consumption per person, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: The household-survey mean (World Bank PIP) in 2024 US$ at market prices, as the site's other builds compute it.

rows.label: Uganda: survey consumption per person, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: As for Kenya.

rows.label: Malawi: survey consumption per person, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: As for Kenya.

rows.label: Zambia: survey consumption per person, 2024 US$
rows.explainer: As for Kenya.

rows.label: Sub-Saharan stand-in: survey consumption per person (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: About $460 a year: the stand-in the site uses for crisis countries with no household survey (South Sudan, Sudan, eastern DRC).

rows.label: Consumption of the people reached, as a share of the stand-in mean
rows.explainer: Food-insecure households in Sudan, South Sudan or eastern DRC consume well under the national survey mean of the stable stand-ins; the poorest fifth in these surveys consume about 40% of the mean. Judgment 55% (35-80%), as in World Vision's model.

rows.label: Consumption per person per year of the people reached in famine-risk settings (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: In market US dollars, like the goods' value, so no PPP factor is needed. The people reached elsewhere have their own row below.

rows.label: Consumption per person per year of the people reached elsewhere (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: The other half (Ukraine, Lebanon and Syria, Myanmar, Jamaica): the site's national-accounts consumption for Ukraine and Lebanon, each times its survey-to-national-accounts ratio (Ukraine's own, Lebanon the world median), at the same crisis-hit share of the mean. Myanmar has no consumption fact; Jamaica's is higher. About $1,700.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person from the food
rows.formula: (famine_setting_share * ln(1 + value_delivered_per_person / (baseline_consumption * years_exposed)) + (1 - famine_setting_share) * ln(1 + value_delivered_per_person / (other_consumption * years_exposed))) * years_exposed
rows.explainer: The food raises consumption over the months it lasts (years_exposed), on the site's one log-income scale, for each setting by its share of the people.

rows.label: Diarrhoeal deaths per person-year where the water points are

source.title: IHME, Global Burden of Disease 2021 results tool (diarrhoeal diseases, Sub-Saharan Africa, all ages, deaths per 100,000)

rows.explainer: The rate a new water supply acts on (most of the 920 points are in Africa: South Sudan, the DRC, Kenya, Ethiopia); wide because the GBD estimate varies by country and year.

rows.label: Share of diarrhoeal deaths a new or repaired water point averts
rows.explainer: Meta-analyses of water interventions (Wolf et al. 2022, Lancet) find large falls in diarrhoea for piped water on premises and chlorination but small, uncertain ones for improved community sources such as boreholes, Samaritan's Purse's main technology; chlorination trials cut child deaths more (Kremer et al. 2023). Judgment 12% (0-30%), as in World Vision's model.

rows.label: Deaths from other causes per diarrhoeal death averted
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared ratio for water treatment.

rows.label: Years a water point serves
rows.explainer: Hand pumps and boreholes last 10-15 years with repairs. Judgment 10 years (5-15).

rows.label: Share of those years the point works
rows.explainer: About a quarter to a third of rural hand pumps in Sub-Saharan Africa are broken at any time (Rural Water Supply Network). Judgment 70% (50-85%).

rows.label: Discounted working years of a water point
rows.explainer: Each year's benefit at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Value of a diarrhoeal death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's age split of diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa (WHO GHE) by the site's values by age.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person given water (before adjustments)
Time saved fetching water, as a share of consumption
rows.explainer: The shared figure for time saved fetching water, mostly women's and girls' (@water.time_saved_consumption_share, 0.75% of consumption, 0-3%).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person from time saved, over the point's life
US households helped by disaster relief and rebuilding in 2025
rows.explainer: Samaritan's Purse helped 5,580 families in 13 disaster deployments (2025 Year-End Report: 'We helped 5,580 families during 13 deployments'), repaired, rebuilt or replaced 144 homes in western North Carolina and dedicated 186 homes in all (Form 990 Part III 4b), and gave $38M of grants to individuals in the US (Part IX line 2), mostly to Helene survivors; at a few thousand dollars a grant that is several thousand more households, some the same. Judgment 9,000 (6,000-15,000).

rows.label: Share of US disaster spending that reaches households as labour, materials, homes or grants
rows.explainer: The rest is staff, travel, the nine disaster relief units, warehouses and volunteers' lodging. The line's grants are $72M of its $185M (Part III 4b), which pass almost entirely to households and rebuilding partners; volunteers' cleanup work has a market value but costs little. Judgment 50% (30-75%).

rows.label: Value delivered per US household (2024 US$)
rows.explainer: About $10,000 a household: a mucked-out house is a few thousand dollars of work, a rebuilt home $150,000 or more.

rows.label: Years the help lasts
rows.explainer: A cleanup lets a family stay or return until permanent repairs; rebuilt homes last decades. Judgment 3 years (1-10), as in Habitat for Humanity's disaster branch.

rows.label: Consumption of the households helped, as a share of the US mean
rows.explainer: Samaritan's Purse rebuilds for uninsured and underinsured homeowners in hard-hit rural areas (western North Carolina, Kerr County, Texas); the poorest fifth of US households spends about 0.67 of the average per person (BLS 2024). Judgment 0.67 (0.5-0.9), as in Habitat for Humanity's disaster branch.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person in households helped, over the years it lasts
rows.formula: ln(1 + us_value_per_household / pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, us_years) / @household_size.united_states / (@united_states.ce_expenditure_per_person_2024 * us_consumption_share)) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, us_years)
rows.explainer: The value spread over its years per person, on the log scale at US consumption: a few thousand dollars means far less to a US household than to a hungry one abroad.

rows.label: Share of medical spending that buys surgery
rows.explainer: The medical ministry's money goes to mission hospitals (grants $14.8M, equipment, $9.6M of volunteer doctors' time, 606 dentists and physicians sent in 2025), the Emergency Field Hospital (Myanmar: 5,800 patients and 332 operations; Jamaica: 4,000 patients and 105 operations, fact sheet), and the cataract (10,000 people since 2017) and cleft (2,300 since 2011) programmes. Surgery is the core of the mission-hospital and volunteer-surgeon work, outpatient care the bulk of the field hospitals' patients. Judgment 50% (30-70%).

rows.label: Full cost of an operation in these hospitals (all funders), US$
rows.explainer: Major operations in African mission and district hospitals cost about $200-1,000 in local costs (Chao et al. 2014 review: $100-1,000 per procedure); flying in volunteer surgeons, equipment and field-hospital logistics cost more. Counting operations as Samaritan's Purse's spending over the full cost gives it its share of all operations, so attribution is 1 here. Judgment $1,500 ($600-4,000).

rows.label: Full cost of an outpatient consultation, US$
rows.explainer: Field-hospital and mission-clinic consultations with drugs; an air-lifted field hospital costs far more per patient than a standing clinic. Judgment $30 ($12-80).

rows.label: Operations funded in 2025
Outpatient consultations funded in 2025
Risk of death without the operation
rows.explainer: Below MSF's 6% for war surgery: mission hospitals operate on obstructed labour, acute abdomens, trauma and burns, but much of the volunteer and programme surgery is elective (hernias, cataracts, cleft lips, orthopaedics). Judgment 3% (1-8%).

rows.label: Share of that risk the operation averts
rows.explainer: As in MSF's model: post-operative mortality is a few per cent. 40% (25-60%).

rows.label: Disability averted per general operation (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Fractures set, hernias and wounds repaired, obstetric fistulas closed: GBD's weights for untreated fractures are 0.1-0.3 for years. 0.3 (0.1-1), as in MSF's model.

rows.label: Share of operations that are cataract or cleft surgery
rows.explainer: About 1,200 cataract operations a year (10,000 since 2017) and 200 cleft repairs (2,300 since 2011, fact sheet) against some 24,000 operations modelled. Judgment 5% (2-10%).

rows.label: Disability averted per cataract or cleft operation, discounted (DALYs)
rows.explainer: Restored sight is worth GBD's blindness weight (about 0.19) for the patient's remaining years, mostly older adults with 8-15 years left, about 1-2 DALYs discounted; a repaired cleft lip lasts a lifetime but its weight is lower. Judgment 1.5 (0.5-4).

rows.label: Disability averted per operation (DALYs)
rows.explainer: General operations and the cataract and cleft operations, by their share.

rows.label: Share of surgical deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Surgical patients are mostly adults (obstetrics, trauma, abdominal surgery). Judgment 10%.

rows.label: Of the surgical deaths averted at five or older, share aged 15-49 (rest 50-74)
rows.explainer: Obstetric and trauma patients are young adults; abdominal and urological surgery older. Judgment 65%.

rows.label: Value of a surgical death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's values by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Share of consultations in field hospitals and crisis clinics
rows.explainer: The Emergency Field Hospital treated about 10,000 patients in Myanmar and Jamaica (fact sheet); most consultations are at mission hospitals and clinics in stable settings (Kenya, Cameroon, Papua New Guinea). Judgment 15% (5-30%).

rows.label: Risk of death without a consultation in a crisis setting
rows.explainer: As in MSF's model for its crisis projects: pneumonia and diarrhoea with dehydration among young children are a small share of consultations. 0.2% (0.07-0.5%).

rows.label: Risk of death without a consultation in a stable setting
rows.explainer: Mission-hospital outpatients in stable countries have other care nearby and fewer acutely ill young children; half MSF's crisis figure. Judgment 0.1% (0.05-0.2%).

rows.label: Risk of death without an outpatient consultation
rows.explainer: Crisis and stable settings by their share.

rows.label: Share of that risk a consultation averts
rows.explainer: Antibiotics and oral rehydration avert most deaths from the treatable conditions, but one consultation doesn't avert all of them (referral, follow-up, late presentation): the low end is a visit that mostly reassures, the high end a sick child treated in time. 30% (15-50%), as in MSF's model.

rows.label: Share of outpatient deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Deaths averted by outpatient care in these settings are mostly young children's (pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria); the low end fits the adult-heavy field hospitals after earthquakes and hurricanes, the high end African clinics. 60% (40-80%), as in MSF's model; the rest valued at ages 15-49.

rows.label: Value of an outpatient death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's values by age band, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Share of the 'children's ministry: other' line spent on the Children's Heart Project
rows.explainer: The line holds the Children's Heart Project and smaller children's projects (restricted 'children's projects - other' $11.5M, p. 20); no split is published. Judgment 60% (35-85%); the rest is valued as material aid below.

rows.label: Spending on the Children's Heart Project
Children given heart surgery in 2025
rows.explainer: The fact sheet counts 'more than 1,680 children' operated on in 88 hospitals since the project began in the late 1990s, about 60 a year on average and more recently. Judgment 70 (40-120).

rows.label: Hospital care donated per child (US$)
rows.explainer: Partner hospitals in the US, Canada and abroad operate free or at cost; US congenital heart surgery is billed at $50,000-200,000, in-country partner hospitals (Uganda, Bolivia) far less. Not in Samaritan's Purse's accounts, so it lowers its share of credit. Judgment $60,000 ($25,000-150,000).

rows.label: Samaritan's Purse's share of the resources behind a heart operation
rows.explainer: Its own cost per child over that cost plus the hospitals' donated care (Convention 2).

rows.label: Risk that a child selected for surgery dies without it
rows.explainer: The project takes children with lesions that need surgery to survive (ventricular septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot); untreated, many die in childhood. Judgment 50% (25-80%).

rows.label: Share of children who survive surgery and do well
rows.explainer: Operative mortality for these repairs is a few per cent in good centres. Judgment 90% (80-97%).

rows.label: Remaining life of a survivor, as a share of a peer's
rows.explainer: Adults after repaired congenital heart disease die earlier than their peers (residual lesions, arrhythmia, heart failure), more so after complex repairs (the low end), little after a closed septal defect (the high end), by the shared rule for survivors' remaining life. Judgment 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: Share of the children under five
rows.explainer: Children are flown in from infancy to early teens; the rest valued at 5-14. Judgment 50%.

rows.label: Value of a child's death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: The site's values by age band, times the survivors' remaining life, times your value of a life.

rows.label: Value of the box's contents to the child, as a share of US retail
rows.explainer: Two parts. Price: the same goods (soap, toothbrush, pencils, notebooks, a T-shirt, small toys) cost well under US big-box retail in local markets; donated clothing resold abroad fetches a fraction of its US price. Use: the child can't choose, and in the one randomised trial of donated goods to children, TOMS shoes for children in rural El Salvador (Wydick, Katz, Calvo, Gutierrez and Janet 2018, World Bank Economic Review, https://doi.org/10.1093/wber/lhw042), most children already owned a pair, so the overall impact was negligible, and the authors report slightly lower shoe purchases in recipient households; in Mexico's randomised food-transfer trial (Cunha 2014, AEJ: Applied, https://doi.org/10.1257/app.6.2.195) the in-kind basket was infra-marginal for total food, but many of its ten items were extra-marginal, given in larger amounts than households would have bought. Judgment 35% (15-60%): half the price gap times most of the goods used, the low end mostly toys displaced or unused, the high end useful items at near local value.
